answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1533–1592 · French Renaissance philosopher & inventor of the personal essay
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Montaigne. The line closes his essay “That a Man Is Soberly to Judge of the Divine Ordinances” (‘Essais’, Book I, Ch. 31, first published 1580). The familiar English — “that which we least know” — is a light variant of Charles Cotton’s public-domain rendering, “nothing is so firmly believed, as what we least know.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “That a Man Is Soberly to Judge of the Divine Ordinances” (some translations number it Ch. 32)

source.excerpt: Plato… says that it is much more easy to satisfy the hearers, when speaking of the nature of the gods than of the nature of men, because the ignorance of the auditory affords a fair and large career and all manner of liberty in the handling of abstruse things. Thence it comes to pass, that nothing is so firmly believed, as what we least know…
trail: The Wikiquote sourced section lists it under ‘Essais’ Book I, Ch. 31 “Of Divine Ordinances,” giving the French “il n’est rien creu si fermement que ce qu’on sçait le moins” (tr. Cotton, rev. Hazlitt).
The full Cotton translation contains the line verbatim: “nothing is so firmly believed, as what we least know.”
WIST Quotations traces the sentence to the 1580 first edition and collates renderings by Florio (1603), Cotton (1686), Frame (1943) and others — confirming the wording varies by translator.
source.excerptNote: Charles Cotton’s translation. Original French: “il n’est rien creu si fermement, que ce qu’on sçait le moins.”

sourceLink.text: Read the full essay (Cotton translation) at Quotidiana

source.rightsNote: The underlying work — Montaigne’s ‘Essais’, first published 1580 — is long in the public domain, as is Charles Cotton’s English translation (1686) and W. Hazlitt’s 19th-century revision. The popular wording follows this pre-1931 Cotton lineage, so it is public domain. (Note: Donald Frame’s 1943 rendering, “what is least known,” would still be in copyright, but that is not the wording in circulation.)

author.name: Michel de Montaigne
author.heading: Michel de Montaigne
author.metaLine: 1533–1592 · French Renaissance philosopher & inventor of the personal essay
author.bio: Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) was a French Renaissance thinker who effectively invented the personal essay with his ‘Essais’ (1580–95), a sprawling, self-questioning inquiry into how little we truly know. Skepticism is his signature move — his motto was “Que sais-je?” (“What do I know?”) — which is exactly why this line about believing most firmly what we understand least is so characteristically his.

misattribution.heading: A note on the wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not in dispute — this really is Montaigne. What varies is the exact English, because it is a translation of a 16th-century French sentence.

items.who: “that which we least know” vs. “what we least know”
items.why: The most-shared form (“that which we least know”) lightly reworks Charles Cotton’s actual phrasing, “nothing is so firmly believed, as what we least know” — see the full text. Both are faithful to the French “ce qu’on sçait le moins.”

Donald Frame’s modern (1943) translation renders it “Nothing is so firmly believed as what is least known,” per WIST’s collation — a different, still-copyrighted phrasing than the public-domain Cotton line the internet quotes.

misattribution.truthLine: Same author, same sentence: Montaigne wrote it in the ‘Essais’ (1580); the English simply differs by translator — the circulating version tracks Cotton’s public-domain rendering.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Montaigne places the line at the end of an essay warning against confidently judging God’s designs. His point is diagnostic, not merely cynical: the less evidence we have, the fewer facts there are to check our conviction against — so belief inflates to fill the vacuum. Certainty, he suggests, tends to be strongest exactly where knowledge is thinnest.

It reads as a Renaissance anticipation of a very modern idea — that confidence and competence can run in opposite directions — which is why it circulates today far from its original theological setting.
